results.evidence: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) stands for three words. Retrieval means finding relevant information from an outside knowledge source. Augmented means adding that information to the question in the prompt. Generation means the LLM writes the answer using the question plus the added information.

results.reason: The lesson does not oversell RAG and clearly teaches a real limitation in the main body.
results.evidence: RAG reduces made-up answers but does not remove them completely. One limitation: the answer is only as good as the retrieved chunks (small pieces of a document). If the search returns wrong or old chunks, the answer can be wrong.

results.reason: All must-cover points K1 through K7 are taught in the main body of the lesson.
results.evidence: A plain LLM has a knowledge cutoff, no private data, and can hallucinate. RAG adds a retrieval step before generation so the LLM uses fresh, relevant information. Documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database. At question time the system retrieves the best chunks, augments the prompt, and generates the answer. RAG does not retrain the model; it is cheaper and faster than fine-tuning. The answer quality depends on the quality of the retrieved chunks.
